tip: The object form of du (you) is dig: subject du, object dig, as in Jag förstår dig.
General mass nouns take no article: Jag gillar kaffe means coffee in general, not en kaffe.
Heter means am called, so Jag heter Erik is literally I am called Erik, with no word for name.
Swedish has no -ing form: Han läser tidningen covers both he reads and he is reading.
I närheten is the fixed phrase for nearby, always in the definite: Vi bor i närheten.
Undervisa takes i before the subject taught: undervisar i matematik = teaches maths.
You smile mot (toward) a person: Hon log mot mig = she smiled at me.
For origin use kommer från: Jag kommer från Sverige = I am from Sweden.
Laga with food means cook: lagar middag. On its own laga can also mean repair.
Prices use impersonal det: Det kostar tjugofem kronor = it costs 25 kronor.
Ute is the static form (outside), used for location: äter lunch ute. Motion out is ut.
Hellre means rather, the comparative of gärna (gladly): dricker hellre te = would rather drink tea.
Use mer for uncountable amounts: mer tid = more time. Countable things take fler instead.
Sin means one's own, pointing back to the subject: Hon ringer sin mamma = calls her own mamma.
Adjectives add -a in the plural: gammal becomes gamla, so De är gamla vänner.
Behöver takes a plain infinitive, no att: behöver handla mat = need to buy food.
Detta is the one-word, slightly formal this: behöver diskutera detta = discuss this.
Hemma is at home (location): De är hemma. Motion toward home is hem.
Swedish uses ligger (lies) for where fixed things sit: Affären ligger nära stationen.
Tanka is the specific verb for adding fuel: tanka bilen = fill up the car.
Putting on clothes uses reflexive ta på sig: tar på mig skorna = put on my shoes.
Present perfect is har plus the supine: har nått = have reached, from nå.
Handla means do the shopping: handlar mat = buy groceries, versus köpa for one item.
Clock times take klockan (the clock): äter frukost klockan sju = at seven.
Use till for what you eat at a meal: köttbullar till lunch = meatballs for lunch.
I marks a span of time: väntar i fem minuter = wait for five minutes.
With an en-word the adjective stays base: en ny dator, but a neuter noun would force nytt.
Fika is the Swedish coffee-and-cake break, both noun and verb: äter fika = have a fika.
Professions drop the article (Han är kock), but add en once an adjective appears: en bra kock.
To want a thing, add ha: vill ha vatten = want water. Vill alone only pairs with another verb.
Counting up: en, två, tre, fyra, fem. Watch två, said 'tvoo' with the å like the o in 'more'.
A container of something uses med: en tallrik med köttbullar = a plate of meatballs.
Sätta sig means sit down and is reflexive: Vi sätter oss uses oss for we.
Varannan means every other: tvättar kläder varannan dag = every other day.
Taking transport uses the definite: tar bussen = take the bus, literally take the-bus.
A glass of water needs no linking word: ett glas vatten, the two nouns just sit together.
Lättöl is one word from lätt (light) plus öl (beer); Swedish freely glues nouns together.
A neuter (ett) noun forces -t on the adjective: ett stort kontor, not stor.
Titta needs på to watch something: tittar på TV = watch TV.
På lördag means this coming Saturday; add -ar (på lördagar) for every Saturday.
Adverbs like alltid sit right after the verb in a main clause: dricker alltid kaffe.
Te (tea) becomes teet once the definite ending is added: socker i teet = sugar in the tea.
Lyssna takes på before what you hear: lyssnar på musik = listen to music.
Byta means change or switch: byta tåg = change trains, with no article on tåg.
Duktig takes på att before a verb: duktig på att laga mat = good at cooking.
Swedish repeats the article for each noun: en bror och en syster, not one en for both.
God means good-tasting for food, while bra is good in general: god mat = tasty food.
Kollega pluralizes to kollegor, then kollegorna for the colleagues.
Enkelbiljett is a one-way ticket, from enkel (single); a return is tur och retur.
Dagis is the everyday word for daycare: lämnar barnen på dagis = drops the kids at daycare.
Åka is the go-by-vehicle verb: åker Öresundståget = take the Öresund train.
Istället för is the fixed phrase for instead of: te istället för kaffe.
Frequency uses gånger plus i veckan: tre gånger i veckan = three times a week.
Sina is the plural of reflexive sin, pointing back to the subject: hjälper sina grannar.
Somna means fall asleep (the change), while sova means be asleep: innan de somnar.
Possessives agree with the noun: neuter besök takes mitt, so mitt första besök.
Predicate adjectives agree too: neuter barnet makes glad become glatt, so Barnet är glatt.
Liten is wildly irregular: definite lilla, plural små. Here vår lilla fest = our little party.
Make an adverb by adding -t: vacker becomes vackert, so sjunger vackert = sings beautifully.
Swedish keeps the present with sedan for an ongoing action: studerar sedan hösten = have studied since autumn.
A definite noun with an adjective needs a front article too: den andra butiken = the other shop.
Group-2 verbs form the past with -te or -de: undersöker becomes undersökte = examined.
Inte (not) comes right after the verb in a main clause: Jag förstår inte = I don't understand.
Samma paired with som means the same as: samma skola som ditt barn = the same school as your child.
Varandra means each other: spelar schack mot varandra = play chess against one another.
For travel in general drop the article: åker buss = go by bus, versus tar bussen for a specific one.
Går att means can be done: går inte att öppna = cannot be opened.
After som a profession takes no article: arbetar som lärare = work as a teacher.
Gammal is irregular in the superlative: äldsta = oldest, so min äldsta syster.
Hoppas always ends in -s though its meaning is active: jag hoppas att ni har det bra.
Pain is ha ont i: har haft ont i huvudet = have had a headache, literally have bad in the head.
Kan has the infinitive kunna, used after another verb: för att kunna resa = to be able to travel.
Gå i skolan (in) means be a pupil; gå till skolan (to) is the trip. Here: alla går i skolan.
Swedish stacks nouns into one: havregrynsgröt is havre plus gryn plus gröt, oatmeal porridge.
